name: Victor Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government, and we don’t sell anything. I’ll keep what you say confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Victor Young, 27, and I lead a small line crew for an electricity company. I check the job pack, then we drive out, isolate the line, climb and replace whatever has failed; the paperwork is usually at the end.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the day do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a fault is fixed and the lights come back, and I’m proud that the crew trusts my calls. Long wet shifts are hard, and the pay is lower than people assume for the risk; I’ve got less than a month of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the new fault-summary tool saves us ten minutes at the depot, but it doesn’t put anyone up a pole. My crew still needs a person to judge the wind and the live equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It probably changes my paperwork, not my hands-on work. I’m still worried about my bank balance because one car repair would eat nearly all my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d try the fault-summary tool on our next few jobs and check every recommendation against the site. I’d keep taking call-outs and put a small amount aside each payday, even if the cushion grows slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI part feels manageable, since I already use tools like that to learn new equipment. The thin savings are what make an ordinary surprise feel sharp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or expense would you notice first if a slow month came along?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d cancel takeaway meals before touching rent or the payment on my used hatchback. My partner Lena and I keep our money mostly separate, so I can’t quietly lean on her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound relaxed about the tool, but you’ve described little room for a bad month. Which weighs more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money pressure weighs more than this small change in software. I’m not expecting fewer hours from the tool, but I know I’m one repair away from borrowing.

say: The **fault summary** saves minutes, but it cannot judge a live line.
A **person on site** still makes the safety call.
think: The software may change **paperwork**, not my climbing work.
My **small savings** leave little room for a car repair.
do: Try the **fault summary** on several jobs and check its notes.
Keep taking **call-outs** and save a little each payday.
feel: I feel **capable** with the tool, but exposed to an ordinary bill.
S0.quote: My crew still needs a person to judge the wind and the live equipment.
fieldNote: Victor distinguishes **site judgment** from clerical help and describes where the tool ends.
His easy tone sits beside **very little savings** and separate household finances.

steps.text: Try the fault-summary tool on three line jobs and check every note
Keep taking call-outs with the current crew
Set aside a small amount from each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that planning software can sort the outage queue faster, but we still have to inspect each site before anyone climbs. If it saves dispatch time, I’d want the freed hours spent on maintenance rather than cutting a position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning and job records could be taken over, and those are part of what makes me a team lead. I think I’d keep a role because I know the lines, though there are few similar employers nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d learn the dispatch and inspection tools our company chooses, then teach the crew how to catch bad site data. I’d also ask my supervisor for more field-lead shifts and keep saving rather than assume the promotion is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about the lead duties disappearing even if the climbing stays. I can adapt, but switching employers would mean a long drive or moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a crew member whose records work had been reduced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell him to show the supervisor what he catches in the field, not pretend the old desk tasks are protected. Then I’d help him find a training slot if the company offers one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would applying elsewhere solve the problem if the same planning tools spread?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not by itself, because other utilities will automate the same records. I’d look at roles with more direct field responsibility, while admitting those roles can change too.

say: AI can speed **outage planning**, while a person checks each site.
I’d use saved time for **maintenance**, not an automatic head-count cut.
think: Planning records are part of my **team-lead work** and could disappear.
My line knowledge may help, but **nearby employers are scarce**.
do: Learn the chosen **dispatch tools** and check their site data.
Ask my supervisor for more **field-lead shifts**.
Save a **portion of each pay** while I watch the staffing plan.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lead duties shrinking, though I can learn quickly.
S1.quote: The planning and job records could be taken over, and those are part of what makes me a team lead.
fieldNote: He recognizes **desk exposure** in his team-lead role and does not claim field knowledge makes it safe.
He leans on field credibility, while acknowledging that **local moves cost money**.

steps.text: Learn the company’s dispatch and inspection tools
Ask the supervisor for more field-lead shifts
Save a portion of each pay while tracking staffing changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say there’s no point pretending the job pack, planning and diagnosis stay ours after 2028. We’d still have about three years before hands-on robots arrive, so the crew’s physical work has a short window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company could automate my lead paperwork almost at once, and then the robots could take the climbing work too. I’d expect a serious risk to my income, not a guaranteed transfer to another crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d use the two years to complete an electrical safety instructor certificate and ask the company whether it will fund it. In the first year after thinking AGI arrives, I’d apply for instructor and inspection posts, knowing their records and diagnoses may also be automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That is frightening because I have no deep cushion and few utilities nearby. I’d sleep badly if my supervisor said our crew was being cut, even though I could start training now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena about the next two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell Lena that I want to take the instructor course while I still have wages, and that we should not sign a bigger lease. I wouldn’t tell her the certificate guarantees a job because it doesn’t.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You’ve named instructor and inspection work, but both involve thinking and records. Could they remain safe after full AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can’t call either one safe after 2028; the system could teach and inspect better too. I’d use those jobs as a possible bridge and keep asking what hands-on work still exists before robots arrive.

say: After **2028**, planning and diagnosis are exposed, not protected work.
The crew gets about **three years** before the stated robot date.
think: My lead paperwork could vanish first, followed by **climbing work**.
A certificate may help me compete, but it offers **no guarantee**.
do: Complete an **electrical safety instructor** certificate before 2028.
Apply for **instructor or inspection posts** in 2029, while checking their exposure.
feel: I feel **worried** about the income risk, but I can start training now.
S2.quote: The company could automate my lead paperwork almost at once, and then the robots could take the climbing work too.
fieldNote: He sees a serious risk across **planning and line work**, but expects no definite layoff yet.
His possible bridge roles are **uncertain**, and he does not treat them as protected careers.

steps.text: Complete an electrical safety instructor certificate before 2028
Apply for instructor and inspection posts during 2029
Avoid signing a larger lease with Lena

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives us time to learn the new equipment and plan safe handovers, not to assume our jobs last forever. The company should tell us how it will handle the 2031 planning shift and the 2034 robot step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d have longer to finish a qualification and build savings than in the 2028 version. Still, if thinking AI takes my records and diagnosis in 2031, I’d have only three years before robots also challenge the line work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask for a training plan and put a fixed amount into savings each month, even if it is small. During 2032, the first year after AGI, I’d apply to field instructor roles and check whether actual vacancies exist before moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious rather than relieved, because there is time but not a clear landing place. Five years makes preparation possible; it doesn’t make the next job appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change in your plan if your employer paid for the qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take the course sooner and keep more cash for rent and transport. I’d still ask for written terms, since a training promise is not the same as a continuing role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a vacancy before knowing whether the role survives AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d only consider it after seeing the work and pay in writing, because moving costs money I don’t have saved. A field post may buy time, but it can be exposed again by 2034.

say: Five years gives time to plan a **safe handover**, not a lifetime guarantee.
The company should explain its **2031 and 2034** staffing plans.
think: I can finish training and build a **small reserve** before 2031.
I still need a real vacancy; **time alone** does not create one.
do: Ask for a written **training plan** and save monthly.
Apply for field instructor work in **2032** after checking vacancies.
feel: I feel **anxious**, because preparation has no guaranteed landing place.
S3.quote: Five years makes preparation possible; it doesn’t make the next job appear.
fieldNote: He turns warning time into **training and modest saving**, while refusing to call it security.
He conditions relocation on a **written offer** and remembers the 2034 physical-work exposure.

steps.text: Request a written lineworker training plan from the company
Put a fixed small amount into savings each month
Check real vacancies before applying for 2032 field instructor posts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade is enough to make deliberate choices, but it isn’t a promise that line crews stay intact. We should use the years to document skills and ask the company what work changes before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This gives me more time to build savings and retrain while I still earn, which matters at 27. But by 2036 the planning and diagnosis are exposed, and three years later the robot date reaches the physical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d take one course at a time in electrical instruction and equipment testing, and move my emergency savings toward three months of bills. In 2037 I’d compare actual instructor openings with the work AI can take over, and apply only if the duties are clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more in control than with a two-year warning, but not secure. A ten-year horizon doesn’t pay next month’s rent or fix my car today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lena notice you doing differently this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She’d see me skip some weekend spending and book the first evening course, not put our lives on hold. We’d keep our current rental while we see whether the course leads to real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rely on teaching or testing as a permanent safe career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, those jobs use judgment and records that AGI can also do. I’d treat them as options to investigate, and keep a second plan if the openings shrink.

say: A decade allows **deliberate preparation**, not a guarantee for line crews.
We should ask what changes before **2036**, while the work is visible.
think: I can build savings and train while I still **earn a wage**.
Instructor and testing work remain **exposed**, so I need another option.
do: Take evening courses in **electrical instruction and testing**.
Build **emergency savings** toward three months of bills.
Compare actual instructor vacancies in **2037** before applying.
feel: I feel **more in control**, but today's bills still weigh on me.
S4.quote: A ten-year horizon doesn’t pay next month’s rent or fix my car today.
fieldNote: More warning brings **agency**, but Victor keeps current financial strain visible in his choices.
He refuses to label adjacent thinking jobs **permanently safe** or assume vacancies will remain.

steps.text: Take evening courses in electrical instruction and equipment testing
Build emergency savings toward three months of bills
Compare instructor vacancies and duties in 2037
Keep the current rental with Lena while testing the course path

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it gives me little time to replace income before robots arrive in 2031. A paid training route, a clear redundancy plan and enough time on wages to build savings would help; none of those guarantees another job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the crew after a machine can climb, not only how accurate the machine is. I’m proud of the work, and I want a straight answer about whether our experience counts when the job changes.

headlineQuote: I’m proud of the work, and I want a straight answer about whether our experience counts when the job changes.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old lineworker** who leads a small crew and enjoys restoring power.
He has **under one month saved** and few nearby employers doing similar work.
He uses technology readily but sees **field judgment** and desk duties as differently exposed.
More warning gives him time to **train and save**, yet he avoids calling a next job guaranteed.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** leaves little time to replace income before robots arrive in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid training route**, clear redundancy terms and time on wages to build savings would help.
